You write and understand a literary story: you alternate passato remoto and imperfetto, and use the trapassato remoto, the narrative participle and gerund, free indirect speech and the historic present.
Aldo reached Florence on the third day, on foot.
It was still raining, and the city was full of mud.
After he had shovelled all day, he sat down on the steps.
Having reached Prato, he asked for a lift.
What was he doing there? Nobody was expecting him.
To alternate passato remoto (actions) and imperfetto (background) in a story.
To recognise and use the trapassato remoto: dopo che ebbe mangiato, appena fu arrivato.
To use the narrative participle and gerund: Arrivato a Prato…, Camminando nel fango…
To recognise and write free indirect speech (the character’s thoughts without “he thought that”).
To use the historic present and nominal sentences for effect.
To use narrative connectors: d’un tratto, fu allora che, non appena, frattanto.
Florence, October. Pietro is writing a story about his grandfather Aldo’s arrival in Florence in 1966. Bellini reads the draft and gives him advice.
The opening is good. But here you wrote: “Aldo è arrivato a Firenze e ha visto il fango.”
It’s fine for a letter. In a story, for a distant tale, you use the passato remoto: “Aldo arrivò a Firenze e vide il fango.”
And the imperfetto? I wrote “pioveva” and “la città era piena di fango”.
Perfect. The imperfetto is the background, the passato remoto is the action. Like in a painting: the landscape and the figure.
And here, when Aldo thinks “What am I doing here?”, do I have to write “pensò che”?
No. Just write: “Che cosa ci faceva lì? Nessuno lo aspettava.” The reader understands that he’s the one thinking it.
As if we were inside his head.
Exactly. It’s called free indirect speech. Verga, Pirandello, Calvino used it. Now you use it too.
Stress on the last syllable: ar-ri-VÒ.
1. Passato remoto and imperfetto in a story
In a story about the distant past, the passato remoto moves the action forward (what happened), while the imperfetto describes the background (what it was like, what was going on meanwhile).
La città era piena di fango.

In Tuscany and in literary texts the passato remoto is very much alive; in northern Italy, in speech, the passato prossimo is used almost always. For a written story, the passato remoto is the natural choice.
2. Trapassato remoto, the narrative participle and gerund
Appena fu arrivato, chiese di lei.
as soon as he had arrived
Arrivato a Prato, chiese un passaggio.
Finito il lavoro, tornò a casa.
Camminando nel fango, pensava a casa.

The trapassato remoto (avere / essere in the passato remoto + participle) appears only after “dopo che, appena, quando, non appena”, when the main verb is in the passato remoto. It’s a literary form: in speech we say “dopo aver mangiato”.
The character’s thoughts enter the story directly, without “he thought that” and without quotation marks. The tenses stay the narrator’s (imperfetto, conditional), but the voice is the character’s.
Aldo pensò: «Che cosa ci faccio qui? Nessuno mi aspetta.»
Aldo si chiese che cosa ci facesse lì, dato che nessuno lo aspettava.
Che cosa ci faceva lì? Nessuno lo aspettava. Sarebbe stato meglio restare a Bologna.
Signs of free indirect speech: questions with no introducing verb, exclamations, the past conditional used as a future (“sarebbe tornato”), the character’s own colloquial words.
4. The historic present and nominal sentences
È il 4 novembre 1966. L’Arno esce dagli argini.
Non c’era luce, non c’era acqua, non c’era pane.
A writer’s tip (Bellini’s): don’t explain emotions, show them. Not “Aldo era triste”, but “Aldo guardò a lungo il pane senza mangiarlo”.
As soon as he arrived, he asked about her.
Walking through the mud, he thought of home.
The work finished, he went home.
Which tense is used for the background?
“Che cosa ci faceva lì? Nessuno lo aspettava.” is:
Aldo reached Florence on the third day.
Di che cosa parla il racconto di Pietro?
Dell’arrivo di Aldo a Firenze nel 1966
Il passato prossimo, da cambiare in passato remoto
Che cosa esprime l’imperfetto, secondo Bellini?
A che cosa paragona Bellini il racconto?
Che cosa permette il discorso indiretto libero?
Di entrare nella testa del personaggio

It was Bellini who suggested it, one evening at the end of September, while they were playing chess in the back of the trattoria. The publisher of his book, “Il fango e la Madonna”, had decided to bring out a new edition for the fourth of November, with restored photographs and one more chapter. Bellini wanted that chapter to be written by someone who hadn’t lived through 1966. “All the voices are in the book,” he said, moving a bishop. “My grandfather Ernesto’s, Graziella’s, those of the mud angels we interviewed. Only one voice is missing. Aldo’s. He’s gone, and nobody has ever told it from the inside. How he felt, what he thought, when he reached Florence that day.” Pietro looked at him without understanding. Bellini pushed the bishop to the other side of the board. “You write it,” he said. “You’re his grandson. You have the black notebook. And you’re sixteen, more or less the age he was. Check.” Pietro looked at the board. It really was check. And, for the first time in his life, he couldn’t find a single question to ask.

The problem was that Pietro knew almost nothing about that day. He knew what everyone in the family knew: that Aldo was born in Bologna in 1948, a printer’s son; that in November 1966 he was eighteen and in his last year of school; that when he heard on the radio that Florence was under water he left without telling anyone; that he arrived on the third day, on foot, by way of Prato; that he shovelled mud in San Frediano for weeks; that he helped Ernesto Bellini carry the fourteenth-century Madonna out of the church; and that on the fourteenth of November, queuing in front of a relief lorry, he gave half his loaf to a twelve-year-old girl called Graziella. But those were facts. They weren’t a story. Pietro didn’t know what the road from Bologna was like, what the weather was, what Aldo ate, where he slept, what he was afraid of. “Then ask,” said Bellini. “The witnesses are still here. Few of them, but they’re here. In a few years they won’t be. It’s now or never.”

The first witness was Graziella. Pietro interviewed her in the kitchen, one Tuesday afternoon, while she was picking over the beans for the next day’s ribollita, because Graziella never talked about important things with her hands still. He asked her to tell him about the fourteenth of November. Graziella sighed. She said she had told it a hundred times already, and that it was all in Bellini’s book, in the chapter “La pagnotta”. Pietro said he knew, but that was her story, the girl’s story. He wanted the boy’s story. What had the girl seen of the boy? Graziella stopped picking over the beans. She thought for a long time. Then she said something she had never said. “His hands were wrecked,” she said. “Not really broken. Full of cuts, of blisters, black with mud up to the wrists. When he gave me the bread, I saw his hands before his face. And I thought: this one isn’t from Florence. Someone from Florence wouldn’t have had hands like that. Someone from Florence, that day, was at home crying. This one had come on purpose to wreck his hands for us.”

Then Graziella remembered something else, which came back to her suddenly while she was putting the beans back in the pot. The boy, when he gave her the bread, had said just one word: “Tieni.” But he had said it in a strange way, with wide, open vowels that nobody in Florence used. “Tîn”, almost. For years, as a child, whenever she thought back to that day, Graziella had heard that word in her head, with that accent, without knowing where it came from. Only eight years later, when Aldo walked into the trattoria and ordered a ribollita, and she heard his voice from the counter, did she understand. She dropped a plate. Her father was angry, because plates cost money. Aldo bent down to pick up the pieces, and she looked at him and thought: it’s him. She didn’t say anything to him for a whole year. “But I knew,” she told Pietro. “I knew from the first word. Write that down. That people recognise each other by their voice before their face.” Pietro wrote it in the black notebook, underlined twice.

The second witness was Efisio, Davide’s grandfather, who was eighty-two, lived in San Frediano and in 1966 had been a Sardinian engineering student who had arrived in Florence two months earlier. Pietro and Davide went to see him one Sunday morning, in the little house where he lived with his wife Lucia, full of black-and-white photographs and shells from Sardinia. Efisio talked for two hours without stopping, his eyes closed, as if he could see everything projected on the inside of his eyelids. He described the noise of the water on the night of the fourth, a noise he had never heard before, like a train that never finished passing. He described the smell the next day: diesel, sewage, rotten wood, and under it all a sweet, terrible smell he never managed to identify. He described the shovels, which at first there weren’t any of, so people dug with their hands, with pots, with drawers from ruined furniture. Pietro wrote everything down. Davide drew. At one point Pietro asked Efisio whether he remembered a boy from Bologna, tall, with a red scarf. Efisio opened his eyes. “There were hundreds of boys from Bologna,” he said. “But a red scarf… Wait.”

Efisio got up, went into the bedroom and came back with a shoebox full of photographs. He spread them out on the kitchen table, among the coffee cups, and began to search, his hands trembling slightly. They were small black-and-white photographs with scalloped edges, taken by a fellow student with a cheap camera. Boys covered in mud up to the waist. Human chains passing buckets. Books hung out to dry on washing lines. A Vespa overturned in the middle of a street. Then Efisio stopped. He picked up a photograph and looked at it for a long time, very close to his eyes. He passed it to Pietro without a word. It showed three boys sitting on the steps of a church, their shovels resting against their knees, dead tired. The one on the left was Efisio, very young, with a moustache and a sailor’s cap. The one in the middle Pietro didn’t know. And the one on the right, with a light scarf round his neck, his black hands resting on his knees and a half-smile, was Aldo. Pietro recognised him at once. He had seen that smile a hundred times, in the wedding photos. But never so young.

“The Bolognese,” said Efisio softly. “That’s what we called him. I never knew his name. We shovelled together for three weeks, in the same street, and never told each other our names. There was no time for names. He had come on foot, I remember, and the first days he had nothing: no boots, no gloves, no shovel. He dug with his hands. On the fifth day I gave him my spare boots, which were two sizes too small, and he put them on anyway and walked around like that for a month.” He stopped. He looked at Pietro, then at the photograph, then at Pietro again. “Was he your grandfather?” he asked. Pietro nodded. He couldn’t speak. Efisio was silent for a long time. Then he said that the Bolognese, on his last day, before going back to Bologna, had returned the boots, cleaned and polished, with a note inside. The note said only: “Thank you. I’ll be back.” Efisio had always thought it was just something people say. “But it was true,” he said. “He came back. For your grandmother.”

Before they left, Efisio asked Davide to make a copy of the photograph. Not a photocopy: a drawing. Davide sat down at the kitchen table and did it there and then, in forty minutes, with a soft pencil, while Lucia made coffee and Efisio went on telling, in fragments, little things that came back to him: the Bolognese who sang while he shovelled, always the same song, whose words he didn’t know; the Bolognese who shared his cigarettes with everyone even though he didn’t smoke; the Bolognese who one day found a porcelain doll in a flooded cellar and washed it with the water from his flask, to give it back to a little girl from the street. Davide drew and listened. When he finished, the three boys on the steps in the drawing were the same as in the photograph, but more alive, as if they were about to stand up. Efisio looked at it for a long time. Then he asked Pietro a favour. “In your story,” he said, “put me in too. Not my name. Just someone who gave him the boots. That’s enough for me.” Pietro promised. And he kept his promise.

Pietro began writing that same evening. He wrote until three in the morning, in his room, with Efisio’s photograph propped against the lamp. The next morning he had six pages. He reread them at breakfast and thought they were awful. He took them to Bellini anyway. Bellini read them in the workshop, sitting on the high stool, his glasses on the tip of his nose and the red pencil in his hand, the same one he had been correcting estimates with for forty years. Pietro watched him read the way you watch a surgeon operating on someone in your family. Bellini said nothing for twenty minutes. Then he looked up. He said the opening was good. That the story was there. But that there was a problem with the tenses. Pietro had written everything in the passato prossimo: “Aldo è arrivato a Firenze e ha visto il fango.” That was fine for a letter, he said, or for telling a friend something. But for a story, for a distant tale from sixty-three years ago, it needed the passato remoto. “Aldo arrivò a Firenze e vide il fango.” Pietro repeated the sentence under his breath. It was the same sentence. But it seemed to come from further away, like a bell heard from the other side of the river.

Bellini explained the rest with the patience with which, years before, he had taught him to clean a brush. In a story, he said, tenses are like the colours of a painting. The imperfetto is the background: the sky, the landscape, the things that last. “It was raining. The city was full of mud. The bells weren’t ringing.” The passato remoto is the figure in the foreground: the action, the gesture, the thing that happens once and changes everything. “Aldo picked up a shovel. Suddenly someone shouted.” If you paint everything in the same colour, the picture goes flat. If you put the figure in the background, nobody sees it. Then he showed him a trick he had learned from his grandfather, who wrote his diary in an elegant, slightly old-fashioned Italian. Instead of writing “when he reached Prato, he asked for a lift”, you could write “having reached Prato, he asked for a lift”. Instead of “while he walked through the mud, he thought of home”, you could write “walking through the mud, he thought of home”. The participle and the gerund, he said, are like quick brushstrokes: they remove the useless words and leave only the movement.

The hardest problem, though, was another one. Pietro wanted to tell what Aldo thought. Not just what he did. In the first version he had written: “Aldo thought that perhaps he had been wrong to come, because nobody was expecting him.” It was correct. But it was cold, like news read out on television. It was Bianca, to whom Pietro gave the second version to read, who found the solution. Bianca had just studied Verga’s “I Malavoglia” at school, and she showed him how Verga did it: he went inside his characters’ heads without saying so, without “he thought that”, without quotation marks. The characters’ questions, doubts and exclamations went straight into the story, with the narrator’s tenses but the character’s voice. “It’s called free indirect speech,” she said. “Try it.” Pietro deleted the sentence and rewrote: “What was he doing there? Nobody was expecting him. In Bologna his mother was surely crying, and his father would say he was reckless. Maybe he was right.” Bianca read it and nodded. “Now I’m inside his head,” she said. “Now I feel cold too.”

That night Pietro read the first thirty pages of “I Malavoglia”, in Bianca’s school edition, full of pencil underlining and notes in the margin in her tiny handwriting. He stayed up until two. He didn’t understand everything: there were Sicilian words, proverbs, sentences that turned round on themselves like waves. But he understood the trick. Verga never said what the fishermen of Aci Trezza were thinking: he let their thoughts come out by themselves, mixed with the narrator’s voice, like fresh water mixing with the sea at the mouth of a river. The next morning he tried rewriting the whole story in Verga’s manner. It was a disaster: Aldo sounded like a nineteenth-century Sicilian fisherman. Bianca laughed until she cried. Then she told him something Pietro never forgot. “You mustn’t write like Verga,” she said. “You must use his tool. The way Davide uses Ernesto’s brush, but paints like Davide.” Graziella, passing by with a basket of vegetables, added without stopping: “Write the way you speak. But better.”

Pietro rewrote the story four times in three weeks. Each version was shorter than the one before, and each version was better. He learned that the most important words were often the ones he took out. He learned that you shouldn’t write “Aldo was sad”, but show it: “Aldo looked at the bread for a long time without eating it.” He learned that a sentence without a verb sometimes said more than a long one: “Mud. Mud everywhere. Mud in the houses, in the churches, in the books.” He learned that the present, suddenly, in the middle of the passato remoto, could have a strange effect, like when the music stops in a film: “It’s the fourteenth of November. There’s a queue in front of the lorry. At the end of the queue there’s a little girl.” Graziella, to whom he gave the third version to read, read it in silence at the kitchen table, with her glasses on, moving her lips. At the end she said nothing. She got up, went to the sink, turned on the tap and started washing a pot that was already clean. Pietro understood that the story worked.

But the next day Graziella made one correction. Just one. She called him into the kitchen at seven in the morning, before Karl arrived, and showed him a sentence on the draft, underlined in pencil. Pietro had written: “He gave her his loaf.” Graziella shook her head. “He didn’t give me all of it,” she said. “He gave me half. He broke it in two, with those wrecked hands, and gave me the bigger half. He kept the other for himself.” Pietro asked whether that was so important. Graziella looked at him the way she did when he got the salt wrong in the broth. “It’s the most important thing of all,” she said. “Anyone can give away something they have too much of. He had nothing extra. He had half a loaf for himself, and he gave me more than half of it. That’s why I married him. Not for the bread. For the bigger half.” Pietro corrected the sentence. “He broke it in two and gave her the bigger half.” Then, after thinking about it, he added a line: “That night, at supper, he ate the smaller half. It seemed to him the best thing he had ever eaten.”

The finished story was twelve pages long. It was called “Il terzo giorno”. It began like this: “It had been raining for four days, and Aldo was eighteen. When the radio said the Arno had burst its banks and Florence was under water, his mother was frying crescentine and his father was reading the paper. Aldo said nothing. Supper over, he went up to his room, put two jumpers, a piece of cheese and the scarf his grandmother had made him into a rucksack, and went out by the back door. It was eleven at night. The road to Florence was long, and he didn’t have a lira.” Bellini read the opening and put down the red pencil. He said there was nothing to correct. Then he read the rest, to the last line, and when he reached the end he took off his glasses and stayed looking out of the workshop window for a long time, towards the roofs of San Frediano. “My grandfather,” he said at last, “would have been happy to be in this story. Even though he only appears in two lines.”

The two lines were these: “In front of the church an old man, his coat soaked through and his glasses broken, was trying to carry out on his own a Madonna taller than himself. Aldo put down his shovel and, without asking anything, took the other end of the panel.” Pietro had rewritten them eleven times. In the first versions there were many more words: the description of the church, the description of the painting, what the two men said to each other. Then he had taken them out one by one, until only the gesture was left. Ernesto Bellini, in his diary, had written only one sentence about that moment: “A boy from Bologna, Aldo, helped me carry the Madonna. We didn’t say a word to each other until she was safe.” Pietro had wanted the same thing in the story: two men who don’t yet know each other, who say nothing, and who carry together something bigger than themselves. Bellini reread the two lines three times. Then he said: “You took out everything that wasn’t needed. It’s the hardest thing there is. In restoration, as in writing.”

The evening before the reading Pietro couldn’t keep still. He reread the story aloud six times in his room, timing himself, until Sara knocked on the door and asked him gently whether he could reread it silently, because Viola, downstairs, was supposed to be sleeping and was instead repeating the sentences by heart. Then Marco came in. He sat on the bed and asked to read it. Pietro hesitated: his father had never read anything he wrote. Marco read the twelve pages in silence, slowly, the way he read his patients’ medical records, without skipping a line. When he finished, he put the pages down on the bed and stayed looking at them for a while. Then he said something Pietro didn’t expect. “I was already a doctor, always on duty, when my father fell ill,” he said. “I never had time to ask him anything about that November. I thought there would be time. Tonight, for the first time, I met him at eighteen.” He stood up, put a hand on Pietro’s head, as he used to when Pietro was little, and left without another word. Pietro stayed awake until dawn, but he didn’t reread the story again.

On the fourth of November, as every year, the mud angels gathered in the church of San Frediano in Cestello. There were fewer and fewer of them: that year, of those who came every year, twenty-three were left, the youngest seventy-seven, the oldest ninety-four. They came from Bologna, Milan, Rome, Germany, England, America. Some walked with sticks, one was in a wheelchair, pushed by a granddaughter. They greeted each other like old schoolmates, with slaps on the back and jokes only they understood. After mass, the publisher presented the new edition of Bellini’s book. And then, as Bellini had asked, he invited Pietro to read the new chapter. Pietro climbed onto the little platform in front of the altar with the twelve pages in his hand, trembling like leaves. He looked at the full church. In the front row were Graziella, Bellini, Efisio and Lucia, Davide with his sketchbook. Further back, Matei and Giulia with Viola, Bianca, Karl, Marco and Sara. Pietro took a deep breath. Then he began to read: “It had been raining for four days, and Aldo was eighteen.”

He read for twenty-five minutes. At first his voice shook, then, little by little, it grew steadier, until Pietro forgot the church, the audience, his hands, and was only the voice of the story. He read the night on the road to Florence, the fruit seller’s lorry that gave him a lift as far as Prato, the walk in the dark from Prato to Florence, with canvas shoes already soaked after a kilometre. He read the arrival at dawn on the third day, from the hill of Careggi: “Florence lay below him, grey, silent, motionless. Not a bell could be heard, not a light could be seen. It looked like a city drawn in pencil and then wetted by a child.” He read the mud. He read the boots two sizes too small. He read the Madonna taller than a man. He read Aldo’s doubts on the first night, sleeping on the floor of a school: “What was he doing there? Nobody was expecting him. Tomorrow he would go home. Tomorrow, for sure.” And then he read: “He didn’t go home. Not the next day, nor the day after that.” In the church nobody coughed. Nobody moved. Twenty-three old angels listened with their heads bowed, each lost in his own third day.

Then Pietro reached the last page, the one with the queue in front of the lorry. He read it in the present, the way he had written it. “It’s the fourteenth of November. There’s a very long queue in front of the relief lorry. Aldo has been queuing for two hours. In his hand he has half a loaf, the one they gave him yesterday. In front of him there’s a little girl with plaits, thin, in a coat too big for her and her father’s rubber boots. She’s twelve. Her name is Graziella, but he doesn’t know that. He won’t know it for eight years. The girl turns round. She looks at the bread. She says nothing. Aldo breaks the bread in two and gives her the bigger half. The girl looks at him, first at his hands, then at his face. Then she takes the bread and runs off, without saying thank you. Aldo stays in the queue with the smaller half. He doesn’t know yet that he has just done the most important thing in his life.” Pietro looked up from the page. He read the last line from memory, looking at the front row. “That night, at supper, he ate the smaller half. It seemed to him the best thing he had ever eaten.”

For a few seconds there was total silence in the church, so deep you could hear the rain beating on the stained-glass windows. Then someone at the back began to clap, and after him everyone else, and the old mud angels rose to their feet, even those with sticks, even the one in the wheelchair, who let his granddaughter help him up. Pietro stood on the platform not knowing what to do with his hands. He looked for his grandmother. Graziella wasn’t clapping. She was sitting in the front row, upright, her hands in her lap, looking at him. Her face was wet, but she didn’t wipe it. When the applause ended and Pietro came down from the platform, she stood up, went to meet him and took his face in her hands, as she used to when he was little. She didn’t say well done, or lovely, or congratulations. She said only, quietly, so that only he could hear: “It was like that. Exactly like that. How did you know?” Pietro didn’t know what to answer. Maybe he didn’t know. Maybe he had only imagined it, with the words the others had given him. Maybe, he thought, that is exactly what telling a story is.

After the ceremony, while the old angels were saying goodbye on the church steps under their umbrellas, a very old man came up to Pietro, leaning on a wooden stick. He was small, stooped, in a felt hat and a light raincoat. He spoke with a strong Bolognese accent. He introduced himself: his name was Gianni, he was eighty-one, and he had come from Bologna by train, as every year. He asked Pietro if he could see Efisio’s photograph, the one with the three boys on the steps. Pietro took it out of the envelope where he kept it. Gianni looked at it for a long time, holding it close to his eyes as Efisio had done. Then he put his finger on the boy in the middle, the one Pietro didn’t know. “That’s me,” he said. “And this one on the right is Aldo. We were schoolmates, in Bologna. We left together, that night. By the back door. He had his grandmother’s scarf and a piece of cheese. I had a bottle of wine and no idea.” Pietro stared at him open-mouthed. In the story he had written that Aldo left alone. Nobody in the family had ever known otherwise.

Gianni laughed when he saw his face. He said it was nobody’s fault. Aldo had never told anyone because, after ten days, Gianni had come down with bronchitis, from the cold and the mud, and had had to go back to Bologna in a Red Cross lorry, and he had always been ashamed of it. “Aldo stayed,” he said. “I didn’t. He became a mud angel. I became someone with a cough.” Then he told them that after 1966 they had lost touch: Aldo had gone to work in Florence, and he had stayed in Bologna and become a printer in the workshop of Aldo’s father, who had no other sons willing to do it. They had seen each other only once more, in 1975, at the wedding. Gianni had been best man. Pietro looked at his grandmother, who had come closer and was listening. Graziella was looking at him as if at a ghost. “The best man,” she said softly. “The boy with glasses who lost the rings in the sacristy.” Gianni blushed like a child. “I found them again,” he protested. “They were in the wrong pocket.” And Graziella, for the first time that day, burst out laughing.

Gianni stayed for dinner at the trattoria. Graziella wouldn’t hear otherwise: the train to Bologna could wait, she said, there was one every hour, whereas a best man came by once every fifty-four years. She sat him at the corner table, the one by Aldo’s plant, and served him the ribollita with her own hands. Gianni tasted it and closed his eyes. He said that Aldo, in Bologna, always talked to him about that soup, in the letters he wrote him in the first years: “the soup of a girl who won’t look at me”. Graziella blushed as if she were twelve. Then she took a loaf from the bread basket, broke it in two in front of everyone, and gave Gianni the bigger half. Gianni looked at the bread, then at her. He understood. He said nothing. He ate in silence, slowly, down to the last crumb. Pietro, sitting next to him, was looking at his hands: they were a printer’s hands, stained with ink even after twenty years of retirement, like those of Aldo’s father in the photographs. He thought that some things don’t wash off. Not ink, not mud, not memories.

That evening Pietro opened the story on the computer and reread it from the beginning. Then he went back to the first page, and to the sentence “went out by the back door” he added three words: “together with Gianni”. Then, further on, he added a whole page: the two boys’ journey through the night, the wine Gianni had brought and which they drank in Prato to warm up, Gianni’s cough getting worse every day, the Red Cross lorry, Aldo walking him to the lorry and saying “Go, I’ll take care of things here”. He sent the new version to the publisher at eleven at night, with a note: “Last correction. A witness who was missing.” The publisher replied after ten minutes: it was too late for the first print run, already printed, but the new page would go into the reprint. Pietro closed the computer and opened the black notebook. At the bottom of the last page, under the date, he wrote: “Today I learned that a story is never finished. There is always a witness you haven’t met yet. You have to leave a door open.” Then, underneath, in red pen, he added: “Like the back door.”
